entities.name: Moses
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Moses (c. 1391–1271 BCE, traditional dating) was the supreme prophet and lawgiver of ancient Israel — the single most consequential figure in the formation of Judaism, and profoundly influential in Christianity and Islam. Born during Pharaoh's genocide of Hebrew male infants, he was hidden in a papyrus basket on the Nile and adopted by Pharaoh's daughter, receiving an Egyptian royal education while retaining his Hebrew identity through his birth mother Jochebed. After killing an Egyptian taskmaster and fleeing to Midian, Moses encountered God in the burning bush on Mount Horeb, receiving the divine name YHWH and the commission to liberate the Israelites. He confronted Pharaoh with ten devastating plagues — culminating in the death of the firstborn and the institution of Passover — then led approximately 600,000 men (plus families) through the miraculously parted Red Sea. During 40 years in the wilderness, Moses served as prophet, judge, military commander, and intercessor: he received the Torah (the 613 commandments) during two 40-day stays on Mount Sinai, oversaw construction of the Tabernacle as God's portable dwelling, organized the twelve tribes, and established the Aaronic priesthood through his brother Aaron. His authorship of the Pentateuch (the Five Books of Moses) gave the Western world its foundational legal, ethical, and narrative framework. Despite leading Israel to the border of Canaan, Moses was denied entry and died on Mount Nebo at age 120, his burial place unknown. The Epistle to the Hebrews calls him faithful in all God's house; Jesus cited his authority; and the Quran names him more than any other prophet (136 times). His legacy shaped three Abrahamic faiths, Western constitutional law (the concept of a supreme written code), and the universal archetype of the liberator.
